title: Book 2 — Euterpe, Chapter 230
paragraphs: If we were to follow the view of the Ionians concerning Egypt — who say that the Delta alone is Egypt, reckoning its seacoast to run from the watchtower called Perseus's to the fish-curing houses of Pelusium, a distance of forty schoeni, and extending inland as far as the city of Cercasorus, where the Nile divides and runs to Pelusium and Canobus, while as for the rest of what we call Egypt, they assign it partly to Libya and partly to Arabia — if, I say, we were to follow this account, we should thereby declare that in former times the Egyptians had no land to live in. For, as we have seen, their Delta at any rate is alluvial, and has only lately come into being (so to speak), as the Egyptians themselves say and as I believe. If then at first there was no land for them to live in, why did they waste their labour trying to prove that they had come into being before all other men? They need not have experimented with children to see what language they would first utter. I am not of the opinion that the Egyptians came into being at the same time as that land the Ionians call the Delta, but rather that they have existed always, ever since the human race came into being, and that as their land advanced forwards, many of them were left in their first dwellings while many came down gradually to the lower parts. At any rate it is certain that in old times Thebes bore the name of Egypt, and the circumference of this region measures six thousand one hundred and twenty furlongs.
